meta.subject: science
meta.description: Astronomy facts: solar system, star lifecycle, moon phases, seasons, galaxies, space exploration, telescopes, Earth in space

facts.statement: The four inner (terrestrial) planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars; they are small, rocky, and closer to the Sun
The four outer planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune; Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter and contains millions of rocky objects
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet by the International Astronomical Union in 2006
Jupiter is the largest planet with a mass more than twice that of all other planets combined
Venus has the hottest surface temperature (about 465 degrees Celsius) due to its extreme greenhouse effect, despite being farther from the Sun than Mercury
The planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun; it has no atmosphere and extreme temperature swings (-180 to 430 degrees C)
Mars is called the Red Planet because of iron oxide (rust) on its surface; it has the largest volcano (Olympus Mons) and longest canyon (Valles Marineris) in the solar system
Saturn has the most prominent ring system, made of ice and rock particles ranging from tiny grains to house-sized chunks
Uranus rotates on its side with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees, making its seasons extreme (each pole gets 42 years of sunlight)
Neptune is the windiest planet in the solar system with wind speeds reaching 2,100 km/h
Earth's revolution (orbit) around the Sun takes about 365.25 days (one year); its rotation on its axis takes about 24 hours (one day)
Comets are icy bodies from the outer solar system that develop tails when near the Sun as ice vaporizes
The Kuiper Belt is a region beyond Neptune containing dwarf planets (including Pluto) and icy bodies
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a massive storm that has been raging for at least 350 years and is larger than Earth
Jupiter has at least 95 known moons, including the four Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto
Europa (moon of Jupiter) and Enceladus (moon of Saturn) are considered candidates for extraterrestrial life because they have subsurface liquid water oceans
The Sun contains 99.86% of the total mass of the solar system
Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon in the solar system with a thick atmosphere and has lakes of liquid methane and ethane on its surface
The Oort Cloud is a theoretical shell of icy objects surrounding the solar system, extending up to 2 light-years from the Sun; it is the source of long-period comets
Dwarf planets include Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, and Ceres (in the asteroid belt); they orbit the Sun but have not cleared their orbital neighborhood

common_errors.wrong: the Sun is the biggest star in the universe
common_errors.correct: The Sun is a medium-sized star (G-type main-sequence). Many stars, like Betelgeuse and UY Scuti, are hundreds of times larger.

common_errors.wrong: Mercury is the hottest planet because it is closest to the Sun
common_errors.correct: Venus is hotter than Mercury (465 degrees C vs 427 degrees C) because Venus has a thick atmosphere that traps heat through the greenhouse effect.

common_errors.wrong: asteroids and comets are the same
common_errors.correct: Asteroids are rocky objects mostly found in the asteroid belt. Comets are icy objects from the outer solar system that develop tails when near the Sun.

common_errors.wrong: Pluto is still a planet
common_errors.correct: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris.

common_errors.wrong: Saturn is the only planet with rings
common_errors.correct: Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have ring systems, though they are much fainter than Saturn's spectacular rings.

common_errors.wrong: the Sun is made of fire
common_errors.correct: The Sun produces energy through nuclear fusion (converting hydrogen to helium), not combustion. Its surface temperature is about 5,500 degrees C.

common_errors.wrong: the planets are close together like in diagrams
common_errors.correct: The solar system is mostly empty space. If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a peppercorn 26 meters away, and Neptune would be nearly a kilometer away.

common_errors.wrong: all planets rotate in the same direction
common_errors.correct: Venus rotates backward (retrograde rotation) compared to most planets, and Uranus rotates on its side. Each planet has its own rotation characteristics.

facts.statement: Stars form from clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, which collapse under gravity
Stars produce energy through nuclear fusion, primarily converting hydrogen into helium in their cores
A star spends most of its life in the main sequence phase, fusing hydrogen in its core
When a massive star exhausts its fuel, it can explode in a supernova, potentially leaving behind a neutron star or black hole
Low-to-medium mass stars (like our Sun) end their lives as white dwarfs after expanding into red giants
A black hole is an object with gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from within its event horizon
The Sun is approximately 4.6 billion years old and is about halfway through its main-sequence life
The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram plots stars by luminosity (brightness) versus temperature (color), revealing stellar evolution patterns
Star color indicates surface temperature: blue/white stars are hottest (over 10,000 K), yellow like the Sun are moderate (~5,800 K), red stars are coolest (~3,000 K)
Red dwarf stars are the most common type of star in the Milky Way, much smaller and cooler than the Sun, and can burn for trillions of years
A neutron star is incredibly dense: a teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth
Elements heavier than iron are primarily created during supernovae; the atoms in our bodies were forged in ancient stars
A planetary nebula is the glowing shell of gas ejected by a dying medium-mass star; it is unrelated to planets despite the name
The more massive a star is, the shorter its lifespan. Massive blue giants may live only millions of years, while red dwarfs can last trillions
The Sun fuses about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second
Stars are born in clusters because nebulae fragment as they collapse; open clusters contain hundreds to thousands of young stars
A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that emits beams of radiation from its magnetic poles; it appears to pulse as it rotates
Binary star systems (two stars orbiting each other) are very common; more than half of all star systems in the Milky Way are binary or multiple star systems

common_errors.wrong: the Sun will explode as a supernova
common_errors.correct: The Sun is too small for a supernova. It will expand into a red giant, shed its outer layers, and end as a white dwarf.

common_errors.wrong: black holes suck everything in like a vacuum
common_errors.correct: Black holes only pull objects in that come close to their event horizon. From far away, their gravity acts like any other object of the same mass.

common_errors.wrong: all stars are the same color
common_errors.correct: Star color indicates surface temperature: blue stars are hottest (~30,000 K), white/yellow are moderate, and red stars are coolest (~3,000 K).

common_errors.wrong: bigger stars live longer because they have more fuel
common_errors.correct: More massive stars burn their fuel much faster and live shorter lives. A star 10x the Sun's mass lives only about 1/1000th as long.

common_errors.wrong: stars twinkle because they are blinking
common_errors.correct: Stars twinkle because their light passes through Earth's atmosphere, which bends and distorts the light due to turbulence.

common_errors.wrong: a supernova destroys everything and creates nothing
common_errors.correct: Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space that become the building blocks for new stars, planets, and eventually life.

common_errors.wrong: our Sun is a small star
common_errors.correct: The Sun is actually larger than about 85% of stars in the Milky Way. Most stars are red dwarfs, which are much smaller and dimmer.

facts.statement: The Moon's phases cycle approximately every 29.5 days: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent
Moon phases are caused by the changing angle of sunlight reflecting off the Moon as it orbits Earth
Earth's seasons are caused by its 23.5-degree axial tilt, not by distance from the Sun
When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun (summer), the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away (winter), and vice versa
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth; a lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
The summer solstice (around June 21) is the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere; the winter solstice (around December 21) is the shortest
Equinoxes (around March 20 and September 22) have approximately equal day and night lengths
Tides are caused primarily by the Moon's gravitational pull on Earth's oceans; the Sun also contributes
Spring tides (highest and lowest tides) occur during full and new moons when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align
Neap tides (least variation) occur during first and third quarter moons when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, meaning the same side always faces us; it takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth
The Moon's diameter is about 3,474 km (about 1/4 of Earth's diameter), and it is about 384,400 km away on average
During a total solar eclipse, the Moon appears to perfectly cover the Sun because the Sun is about 400 times larger but also about 400 times farther away
The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no wind, weather, or sound on its surface; footprints left by astronauts may last millions of years
Waxing means the illuminated portion is increasing (right side in Northern Hemisphere); waning means it is decreasing
The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 cm per year due to tidal interactions
Day and night are caused by Earth's rotation on its axis; the side facing the Sun experiences day while the opposite side experiences night

common_errors.wrong: seasons are caused by Earth being closer to or farther from the Sun
common_errors.correct: Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt. Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun during Northern Hemisphere winter.

common_errors.wrong: the Moon produces its own light
common_errors.correct: The Moon reflects sunlight. It does not produce its own light. The different phases show how much of the lit side we can see.

common_errors.wrong: there is a permanent dark side of the Moon
common_errors.correct: All sides of the Moon receive sunlight. The far side is always facing away from Earth due to tidal locking, but it is not permanently dark.

common_errors.wrong: the Moon controls the tides by magnetism
common_errors.correct: Tides are caused by gravitational pull, not magnetism. The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, creating tidal bulges.

common_errors.wrong: eclipses happen every month
common_errors.correct: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun, so eclipses only occur when the orbits align, a few times per year.

common_errors.wrong: a lunar eclipse is dangerous to look at
common_errors.correct: A lunar eclipse is safe to view with the naked eye. It is a SOLAR eclipse that is dangerous to look at directly because of the Sun's intense light.

common_errors.wrong: the Moon is always the same distance from Earth
common_errors.correct: The Moon's orbit is elliptical. At perigee it is about 356,500 km away; at apogee about 406,700 km. This causes supermoons and micromoons.

facts.statement: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, approximately 9.46 trillion kilometers (5.88 trillion miles)
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a barred spiral galaxy containing an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars
The three main types of galaxies are spiral, elliptical, and irregular
The Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away
The Big Bang theory states that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since
The observable universe contains an estimated 2 trillion galaxies
The Milky Way galaxy is about 100,000 light-years in diameter and our Sun is located about 26,000 light-years from the center
Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe and dark energy about 68%; ordinary matter we can see is only about 5%
Edwin Hubble discovered that the universe is expanding: galaxies farther from us are moving away faster (Hubble's Law)
Redshift occurs when light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths as the universe expands, shifting toward the red end of the spectrum
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is faint radiation left over from the Big Bang, discovered in 1965, and provides evidence for the Big Bang theory
The Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies are expected to collide and merge in about 4.5 billion years
The nearest star to our Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years away
An astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km (93 million miles)
A supermassive black hole lies at the center of most galaxies, including the Milky Way; ours is called Sagittarius A* and has a mass of about 4 million Suns
Galaxies are organized into clusters and superclusters; the Milky Way is part of the Local Group, which contains about 80 galaxies

common_errors.wrong: a light-year measures time, not distance
common_errors.correct: A light-year is a unit of distance, not time. It is the distance light travels in one year.

common_errors.wrong: the Big Bang was an explosion in space
common_errors.correct: The Big Bang was not an explosion in existing space. It was the rapid expansion of space itself from an extremely hot, dense state.

common_errors.wrong: the North Star (Polaris) is the brightest star in the sky
common_errors.correct: Sirius is the brightest star visible from Earth. Polaris is relatively faint but important because it marks celestial north.

common_errors.wrong: we can see the entire universe
common_errors.correct: We can only see the observable universe (about 93 billion light-years across). Light from beyond has not had time to reach us since the Big Bang.

common_errors.wrong: the universe is expanding into something
common_errors.correct: The universe is not expanding into anything. Space itself is expanding. There is no edge or boundary that we know of.

common_errors.wrong: stars in a constellation are close together in space
common_errors.correct: Stars in a constellation appear close together from Earth but are usually at vastly different distances from us.

common_errors.wrong: the Milky Way is the only galaxy
common_errors.correct: There are an estimated 2 trillion galaxies in the observable universe. The Milky Way is just one among them.

facts.statement: The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961, orbiting Earth in Vostok 1
Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission
The International Space Station (ISS) orbits Earth at about 408 km altitude and travels at roughly 28,000 km/h, completing an orbit every 90 minutes
The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits above Earth's atmosphere and has provided some of the most detailed images of distant galaxies
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in 2021, uses infrared to see farther into space and time than Hubble
Mars rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance) have explored Mars's surface, studying geology, climate, and searching for signs of past water and life
Voyager 1 and 2, launched in 1977, are the farthest human-made objects from Earth; Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012
A satellite is any object that orbits another object; the Moon is a natural satellite of Earth, while the ISS is an artificial satellite
Rockets work by Newton's Third Law: exhaust gases are pushed downward, and the rocket is pushed upward as an equal and opposite reaction
Astronauts experience weightlessness (microgravity) in orbit because they are in continuous free fall around Earth, not because there is no gravity
The speed needed to stay in orbit around Earth (orbital velocity) is about 28,000 km/h; escape velocity from Earth is about 40,270 km/h
Reusable rockets developed by SpaceX have significantly reduced the cost of reaching orbit by landing and reflying first-stage boosters
The Artemis program aims to return humans to the Moon and establish a sustainable presence there as a stepping stone toward Mars exploration
Space telescopes observe from above Earth's atmosphere, which blocks or distorts many types of electromagnetic radiation including infrared, ultraviolet, and X-rays

common_errors.wrong: there is no gravity in space
common_errors.correct: Gravity exists everywhere in space. Astronauts on the ISS feel weightless because they are in free fall (constantly falling around Earth), not because gravity is absent.

common_errors.wrong: the Space Shuttle is still in use
common_errors.correct: NASA's Space Shuttle program ended in 2011. Currently, astronauts reach the ISS on SpaceX Crew Dragon and Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

common_errors.wrong: we have sent humans to Mars
common_errors.correct: As of 2026, no humans have traveled to Mars. Only robotic rovers and landers have explored Mars's surface.

common_errors.wrong: satellites stay in space without any force acting on them
common_errors.correct: Satellites are held in orbit by gravity. They are moving fast enough sideways that they continuously fall around Earth without hitting the surface.

common_errors.wrong: the first person in space was American
common_errors.correct: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin was the first human in space (April 12, 1961). American Alan Shepard followed on May 5, 1961.

common_errors.wrong: space is completely empty
common_errors.correct: Space contains dust, gas, cosmic rays, radiation, dark matter, and dark energy. It is not completely empty, though it is far less dense than any environment on Earth.

facts.statement: Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, causing day and night
Earth revolves around the Sun once every 365.25 days; the extra quarter day is why we have a leap year every 4 years
Earth's atmosphere is composed of about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases including argon and carbon dioxide
Earth's magnetic field is generated by the movement of molten iron in its outer core; it protects us from harmful solar radiation and solar wind
The aurora borealis (Northern Lights) and aurora australis (Southern Lights) are caused by charged particles from the Sun interacting with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere
A meteor is a streak of light caused by a small space rock burning up in Earth's atmosphere; if it reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite
Earth is the only known planet to have liquid water on its surface, which is essential for life as we know it
The heliocentric model (Sun-centered) replaced the geocentric model (Earth-centered); Copernicus proposed it and Galileo provided supporting evidence
Earth is approximately 4.54 billion years old, as determined by radiometric dating of rocks and meteorites
Earth's layers from outside to inside are: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid iron), and inner core (solid iron)
The Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west because Earth rotates from west to east
Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in orbit and holds our atmosphere in place; gravity decreases with distance from Earth's center

common_errors.wrong: the Sun moves around the Earth
common_errors.correct: Earth orbits the Sun, not the other way around. The Sun appears to move across the sky because Earth rotates on its axis.

common_errors.wrong: we have seasons because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
common_errors.correct: Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt, which changes how directly sunlight hits different parts of Earth throughout the year.

common_errors.wrong: shooting stars are actual stars falling from the sky
common_errors.correct: Shooting stars (meteors) are small pieces of space debris burning up in Earth's atmosphere. They are not stars at all.

common_errors.wrong: Earth is a perfect sphere
common_errors.correct: Earth is an oblate spheroid: it is slightly flattened at the poles and wider at the equator due to its rotation.

common_errors.wrong: the North Star has always been the North Star
common_errors.correct: Earth's axis slowly wobbles (precession) over a 26,000-year cycle. Different stars serve as the North Star at different times in this cycle.

facts.statement: The Sun is a medium-sized yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence) with a surface temperature of about 5,500 degrees Celsius
The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium at temperatures of about 15 million degrees Celsius
The Sun is composed of approximately 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with the remaining 2% being heavier elements
Sunspots are cooler, darker areas on the Sun's surface caused by intense magnetic activity; they follow an approximately 11-year cycle
Solar flares are sudden eruptions of energy from the Sun's surface that can disrupt communications and power grids on Earth
The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun at speeds of 400-800 km/s
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, traveling at 300,000 km/s
The Sun's corona (outer atmosphere) is visible during total solar eclipses and is paradoxically hotter (1-2 million degrees C) than the surface (5,500 degrees C)
The Sun is about 109 times the diameter of Earth and could fit about 1.3 million Earths inside it
The Sun provides virtually all the energy that drives weather, ocean currents, and life on Earth through light and heat

common_errors.wrong: the Sun is on fire
common_errors.correct: The Sun is not burning like a fire. It produces energy through nuclear fusion, not combustion. There is no oxygen in the Sun to support burning.

common_errors.wrong: the Sun will burn forever
common_errors.correct: The Sun has a limited fuel supply. In about 5 billion years, it will exhaust its hydrogen fuel, expand into a red giant, and eventually become a white dwarf.

common_errors.wrong: the Sun is yellow
common_errors.correct: The Sun actually emits white light (all colors). It appears yellow from Earth because our atmosphere scatters shorter blue wavelengths, making the remaining light look yellow.

common_errors.wrong: sunspots are holes in the Sun
common_errors.correct: Sunspots are cooler regions on the Sun's surface caused by magnetic field concentrations. They are still extremely hot (about 3,500 degrees C), just cooler than the surrounding surface.

common_errors.wrong: the Sun is the same temperature everywhere
common_errors.correct: The Sun's temperature varies enormously: the core is about 15 million degrees C, the surface is about 5,500 degrees C, and the corona exceeds 1 million degrees C.

facts.statement: A constellation is a pattern of stars as seen from Earth; the International Astronomical Union recognizes 88 official constellations
Polaris (the North Star) appears almost directly above Earth's North Pole, making it useful for navigation; it is part of the constellation Ursa Minor
The Big Dipper is an asterism (recognizable star pattern) within the constellation Ursa Major; its pointer stars help locate Polaris
Galileo Galilei was the first to use a telescope for astronomical observations (1609), discovering Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, and craters on the Moon
Apparent magnitude measures how bright a star appears from Earth; absolute magnitude measures its true brightness. A lower number means brighter
Stars visible in the night sky change with the seasons because Earth's orbit around the Sun shifts our nighttime view to different parts of the sky

common_errors.wrong: constellations are fixed groups of stars that are physically close together
common_errors.correct: Constellations are patterns we see from Earth. The stars in a constellation are usually at very different distances from us and are not physically related.

common_errors.wrong: telescopes make stars look bigger
common_errors.correct: Stars are so far away they always appear as points of light, even through telescopes. Telescopes gather more light, making stars appear brighter and revealing fainter objects.

common_errors.wrong: you can only see planets with a telescope
common_errors.correct: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are all visible to the naked eye. They appear as bright, non-twinkling points of light in the night sky.
